blocks.body:
A pile has $21$ stones. Two players take turns removing $1$, $2$ or $3$ stones, and whoever takes the last stone wins. The first player can force a win: take $1$ stone, leaving $20$, and from then on, whenever the opponent takes $k$ stones, take $4-k$. The pile then always has a multiple of $4$ stones after the first player's move, and in particular the first player takes the last stone.

This lesson is about games of this kind: two players, alternating moves, no chance, no hidden information. Who wins with best play, and how? The tools are the classification of positions as winning or losing, symmetry and pairing strategies, strategy stealing, and the Sprague–Grundy theory, which turns any such game into a single heap of Nim.

blocks.title: The setting
blocks.body:
We study impartial games: from every position both players have the same moves available (so chess, where each side moves only its own pieces, is not impartial). We use the normal play convention: a player who cannot move loses. And we assume the game is finite: from a given starting position only finitely many positions can arise, and no position can ever occur twice in a play. Then every play ends after fewer moves than there are positions. In practice finiteness is usually proved with a monovariant, such as the total number of stones (see [[invariants]]).

It helps to picture the positions as the vertices of a directed graph, with an arrow $P \to Q$ whenever one move turns $P$ into $Q$. We call $Q$ an option of $P$. A position with no options is terminal, and the player to move there loses.

blocks.title: P-positions and N-positions
blocks.body:
A position is an N-position if the player about to move (the Next player) can force a win, and a P-position if the player who just moved (the Previous player) can force a win, whatever the opponent does.

So in the opening game a pile of $20$ is a P-position and a pile of $21$ is an N-position.

blocks.title: Every position is winning or losing
blocks.body:
In a finite impartial game under normal play, every position is either a P-position or an N-position, and:

1. a position is a P-position exactly when every option of it is an N-position (in particular, terminal positions are P-positions);
2. a position is an N-position exactly when it has at least one option that is a P-position.

Moreover, if a set $Z$ of positions contains every terminal position, has no move from a position in $Z$ to another position in $Z$, and allows a move into $Z$ from every position outside $Z$, then $Z$ is exactly the set of P-positions.

Give each position its height: the length of the longest play starting from it. Heights are finite because the game is finite, and every option of a position has smaller height.

Label positions in order of increasing height: terminal positions (height $0$) get the label P; a position of larger height gets N if some option is labelled P, and P otherwise. Each option has smaller height, so it is already labelled when we need it. This labelling satisfies rules 1 and 2, and an induction on height shows that a labelling satisfying them is unique; the same induction shows that any set $Z$ with the three stated properties coincides with the P-labelled set.

It remains to see that the labels describe who wins. A player facing an N-label moves to a P-labelled option. The opponent then faces P, and every move from there leads to N. So the first player can always move to P again. The heights keep dropping, and eventually the opponent faces a terminal position and loses. A player facing P is in the opposite situation: whatever they do, the opponent faces N and wins as just described.

blocks.title: Small cases and the subtraction game
blocks.body:
In the opening game (remove $1$, $2$ or $3$), compute labels from the bottom: $0$ stones is terminal, so P. Piles $1, 2, 3$ can move to $0$, so N. A pile of $4$ can only reach $3, 2, 1$, all N, so it is P. The pattern repeats: a pile of $n$ is a P-position exactly when $4 \mid n$. To prove it, use the characterisation with $Z = \{n : 4 \mid n\}$. From a multiple of $4$, removing $1$, $2$ or $3$ never gives a multiple of $4$; from any other $n$, removing $n \bmod 4$ gives one.

This tiny case shows the general routine: compute labels from small positions upward to guess the answer, then prove the guess by checking that you cannot move inside $Z$ and that from outside you can always move into it. The winner keeps the game inside $Z$ after each of their own moves, exactly as one maintains an invariant.

blocks.title: Symmetry, pairing and strategy stealing
blocks.body:
Many games are won by copying. Two players alternately place equal round coins on a rectangular table, without overlap and without hanging off the edge; whoever cannot place a coin loses. The first player wins: put the first coin exactly at the centre, and afterwards answer each coin by its mirror image through the centre. After each of the first player's moves the arrangement is centrally symmetric, so the mirror position of the opponent's new coin is free of the earlier coins; it cannot overlap the opponent's new coin either, since two mirror-image coins overlapping would mean both overlap the central one. Pairing strategies are the same idea in discrete form: split the possible moves into pairs and always answer a move with its partner. For instance, if a move knocks down one pin or two adjacent pins from a row, the first player wins by removing the middle one or two pins and then mirroring the opponent's moves in the other half.

Strategy stealing is non-constructive. To show the first player wins, assume instead that the second player has a winning strategy. If the first player can make some harmless move and then play as the second player, following that strategy, they win, a contradiction since both cannot have winning strategies. The argument needs an extra move that can never hurt, and it proves a winning strategy exists without describing it.

blocks.title: Nim
blocks.body: In Nim there are several heaps of stones. A move takes any positive number of stones from one heap. Whoever takes the last stone wins. Write the heap sizes in binary and add them without carrying: this is the bitwise exclusive or, written $\oplus$ and called the nim-sum. For example $3 \oplus 5 = 011_2 \oplus 101_2 = 110_2 = 6$. The operation is associative and commutative, $a \oplus a = 0$ and $a \oplus 0 = a$.

blocks.title: Bouton's theorem
blocks.body:
A Nim position with heaps $n_1, \dots, n_k$ is a P-position if and only if
$$n_1 \oplus n_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus n_k = 0.$$

Let $Z$ be the set of positions with nim-sum $0$ and use the characterisation theorem. The terminal position (all heaps empty) has nim-sum $0$.

From $Z$ a move changes one heap $n_i$ to some $n_i' \ne n_i$, so the nim-sum changes from $s = 0$ to $s \oplus n_i \oplus n_i' \ne 0$. No move stays in $Z$.

From a position with nim-sum $s \ne 0$, let $2^j$ be the highest power of $2$ in the binary expansion of $s$. Some heap $n_i$ has a $1$ in position $j$, since otherwise $s$ would have $0$ there. The number $n_i \oplus s$ agrees with $n_i$ above position $j$ and has $0$ at position $j$, so $n_i \oplus s < n_i$. Reduce heap $i$ to $n_i \oplus s$. The new nim-sum is $s \oplus n_i \oplus (n_i \oplus s) = 0$, so this move enters $Z$.

blocks.title: Sprague–Grundy values
blocks.body:
Every impartial game behaves, as a component of a sum, exactly like a single Nim heap of a suitable size. For a finite set $A$ of non-negative integers, $\operatorname{mex} A$ (minimum excluded value) is the least non-negative integer not in $A$; for instance $\operatorname{mex}\{0,1,3\} = 2$ and $\operatorname{mex}\varnothing = 0$. The Grundy value of a position is defined from the bottom up by
$$\mathcal G(P) = \operatorname{mex}\{\mathcal G(Q) : P \to Q\}.$$
By the definition of mex, $\mathcal G(P) = 0$ exactly when no option has value $0$, so by the characterisation theorem the positions of value $0$ are precisely the P-positions. A Nim heap of size $n$ has options of sizes $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, so by induction its value is $n$.

The sum $P_1 + P_2$ of two games is played by putting both boards side by side; a move consists of a move in exactly one of them, and a player who cannot move in either loses. A Nim position is a sum of single heaps.

blocks.title: Sprague–Grundy theorem
blocks.body:
For positions $P_1, P_2$ of finite impartial games,
$$\mathcal G(P_1 + P_2) = \mathcal G(P_1) \oplus \mathcal G(P_2).$$
Consequently a sum of games is a P-position exactly when the nim-sum of the Grundy values of its components is $0$.

Induct on the sum of the heights of $P_1$ and $P_2$. Write $a = \mathcal G(P_1)$, $b = \mathcal G(P_2)$, $g = a \oplus b$. The options of $P_1 + P_2$ are $Q_1 + P_2$ and $P_1 + Q_2$ with $P_1 \to Q_1$ or $P_2 \to Q_2$, and by induction their values are $\mathcal G(Q_1) \oplus b$ and $a \oplus \mathcal G(Q_2)$. We must show that $g$ is not among these values and every $h < g$ is.

The value $g$ does not occur: $a$ is the mex of the values of options of $P_1$, so $\mathcal G(Q_1) \ne a$ and hence $\mathcal G(Q_1) \oplus b \ne a \oplus b$. The same holds for moves in $P_2$.

Every $h < g$ occurs: let $d = g \oplus h$ and let $2^j$ be its highest binary digit. Because $h < g$, at position $j$ the number $g$ has a $1$ and $h$ has a $0$. Since $g = a \oplus b$, exactly one of $a$, $b$ has a $1$ at position $j$; say $a$. Then $a' = a \oplus d$ is less than $a$, because it agrees with $a$ above position $j$ and has a $0$ there. As $a$ is a mex, some option $Q_1$ of $P_1$ has $\mathcal G(Q_1) = a'$, and the option $Q_1 + P_2$ has value $a' \oplus b = a \oplus b \oplus d = g \oplus d = h$.

Applying the theorem repeatedly handles any number of components, and the final statement follows because value $0$ means P-position.

blocks.title: Winning moves in Nim
blocks.body: In Nim with heaps $3, 5, 7$, who wins, and what are all the winning first moves?
blocks.solution:
In binary $3 = 011$, $5 = 101$, $7 = 111$, and the nim-sum is $011 \oplus 101 \oplus 111 = 001 = 1$. It is non-zero, so the first player wins.

A winning move replaces some heap $n_i$ by $n_i \oplus 1$, which must be smaller than $n_i$. Every heap here is odd, so $n_i \oplus 1 = n_i - 1$ works for each. The winning moves are $3 \to 2$, $5 \to 4$ and $7 \to 6$: take one stone from any heap. Each leaves nim-sum $0$, for example $2 \oplus 5 \oplus 7 = 010 \oplus 101 \oplus 111 = 000$. No other move works, since the only move leaving nim-sum $0$ from heap $n_i$ is to $n_i \oplus 1$.

blocks.title: A sum of subtraction games
blocks.body: In the subtraction game $S = \{1, 3, 4\}$, a move removes $1$, $3$ or $4$ stones from a pile. Three piles of $10$, $11$ and $12$ stones are played as a sum: each move removes $1$, $3$ or $4$ stones from one pile, and whoever cannot move loses. Who wins?
blocks.solution:
Compute Grundy values $g(n)$ of a single pile from the bottom, using $g(n) = \operatorname{mex}\{g(n-s) : s \in S, s \le n\}$:
$$g(0)=0,\ g(1)=\operatorname{mex}\{0\}=1,\ g(2)=\operatorname{mex}\{1\}=0,\ g(3)=\operatorname{mex}\{0,0\}=1,$$
$$g(4)=\operatorname{mex}\{1,1,0\}=2,\ g(5)=\operatorname{mex}\{2,0,1\}=3,\ g(6)=\operatorname{mex}\{3,1,0\}=2,\ g(7)=\operatorname{mex}\{2,2,1\}=0.$$
Continuing, $g(8) = \operatorname{mex}\{0,3,2\} = 1$, $g(9) = \operatorname{mex}\{1,2,3\} = 0$ and $g(10) = \operatorname{mex}\{0,0,2\} = 1$, so $g(7), \dots, g(10)$ equal $g(0), \dots, g(3)$. For $n \ge 11$ all three moves are available both from $n$ and from $n - 7$, and $g(n)$ is computed from $g(n-1), g(n-3), g(n-4)$ in the same way that $g(n-7)$ is computed from $g(n-8), g(n-10), g(n-11)$. By induction on $n$ these inputs agree, so $g(n) = g(n-7)$. Hence $g$ has period $7$ with pattern $0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 2$.

Hence $g(10) = g(3) = 1$, $g(11) = g(4) = 2$ and $g(12) = g(5) = 3$. By the Sprague–Grundy theorem the sum has value $1 \oplus 2 \oplus 3 = 0$, so it is a P-position: the second player wins.

blocks.title: Chomp
blocks.body: A chocolate bar is an $m \times n$ grid of squares with $mn > 1$, and the bottom-left square is poisoned. Players alternately choose a remaining square and eat it together with every remaining square above it and to the right of it (weakly). Whoever eats the poisoned square loses. Prove that the first player has a winning strategy.
blocks.solution:
Treat taking the poisoned square as not allowed, so a player facing only the poisoned square cannot move and loses. Every move removes a square, so the game is finite and one of the players has a winning strategy.

Suppose the second player has one. Let the first player open by eating only the top-right square. The second player has a winning reply: eat the cone of some square $s$ (that is, $s$ and everything above and to the right of it). The top-right square lies in every cone, so the bar left after these two moves is the full bar minus the cone of $s$. Because that reply wins, this position is a P-position: the player to move from it loses. But the first player could have produced exactly this position with the single opening move $s$. So the starting bar has an option that is a P-position, which makes it an N-position, and the first player wins after all. This contradicts the assumption, so the first player has the winning strategy.

The argument says nothing about which first move wins; for general rectangles no simple description of it is known.

blocks.body:
- The nim-sum is not the ordinary sum. Heaps $1, 2, 3$ have total $6$ but nim-sum $0$, so they form a P-position.
- Grundy theory needs impartial games and normal play. In misère Nim, where taking the last stone loses, the rule changes: when every heap has at most one stone, the player to move wins exactly when the number of non-empty heaps is even; otherwise the ordinary nim-sum rule still applies.
- Infinite games and games with draws are outside this theory; finiteness has to be checked, usually with a monovariant.
- A symmetry strategy must also handle moves that touch the centre; that is why the first coin in the table game goes at the centre.

The set of P-positions is an invariant in the sense of [[invariants]]: the winning player keeps returning the game to it. Nim-sums are binary arithmetic without carries, so [[digits-bases]] is the right language for computing them. The game graph is a directed graph without cycles, and many games are played on graphs (see [[graph-basics]]).

Beyond impartial games, Conway's theory of partizan games assigns to positions values in a large partially ordered group that contains the surreal numbers. On the computational side, deciding the winner of natural games played on large boards, such as generalised Hex, is PSPACE-complete, a class believed to be even harder than NP (see [[p-vs-np]]).

1. Find all winning first moves in Nim with heaps $2, 5, 6, 9$.
2. Compute the Grundy values of the subtraction game with $S = \{1, 2, 4\}$ and find their period.
3. Give an explicit winning strategy for the first player in Chomp on an $n \times n$ square bar.
4. Prove the misère Nim rule stated in the pitfalls.
